quote: Welche Sin- gularitäten in $\lambda$ sind möglich?
english: Which singularities in λ are possible?
topic: Hilbert discusses the dependence of solutions of differential equations on a parameter λ, noting that they have poles at the special values of λ, and asks general questions about singularities and branching in the parameter and about whether the coefficient A(x) is determined by the singular values.

triage.modern_statement: Take a linear ODE (most likely of Sturm–Liouville type, e.g. y'' + (λ + A(x)) y = 0, with boundary conditions) whose coefficients depend analytically on a complex parameter λ. Hilbert asks what kind of singularities the λ-dependent solution can have, as a function of λ. He has already noted poles at the special values (eigenvalues); the question is whether essential singularities or branch points can also occur. In modern terms: describe the analytic structure in λ of the solutions and of the boundary-value solution (the Green's function or resolvent). The standard answer is this. Solutions fixed by initial conditions are entire (or holomorphic) in λ, by Poincaré's theorem on analytic dependence on parameters. The solution of the boundary-value problem, i.e. the resolvent, is meromorphic in λ. It is a ratio of entire functions, as in Fredholm's theory, and its only singularities are poles at the eigenvalues. A general modern form is the analytic Fredholm theorem.
triage.answered_by: The core result was largely already known or arriving around Hilbert's time. Poincaré (1890s) showed that ODE solutions depend analytically on parameters. Fredholm (1903) and Hilbert himself (Grundzüge einer allgemeinen Theorie der linearen Integralgleichungen, 1904–1910) showed that the resolvent is a ratio of entire functions, so it is meromorphic in λ with poles only at the eigenvalues. This was later generalised as the analytic Fredholm theorem. The related question on the same page, whether A(x) is determined by the singular values, became the inverse Sturm–Liouville problem. Ambarzumian (1929) and Borg (1946) answered it: in general two spectra are needed. Gelfand–Levitan and Marchenko developed it further in the 1950s. Note: the Fredholm/Hilbert attributions and dates come from general knowledge; no search result checked here confirms them.

evidence.claim: Poincaré's theorem: solutions of differential equations are analytic in the initial conditions and in parameters, provided the right-hand sides are analytic.
Poincaré established that solutions of differential equations are frequently analytic functions of initial conditions and parameters.
The Fredholm resolvent is written as a ratio N(λ)/σ(λ), which gives its meromorphic structure in λ. The analytic Fredholm framework gives meromorphic dependence on λ.
Modern analytic Fredholm theory shows meromorphy of operator-valued functions of λ.

Related question (is A(x) determined by the singular values?): Ambarzumian (1929) recovered the zero potential from one spectrum. Borg (1946) proved the foundational theorem that potentials are determined by spectral data, in general needing two spectra.
Borg showed that one spectrum is not enough in general and two spectra are needed to determine the potential uniquely.

triage.why: The note is short, but the page context (λ-dependence, poles at the special values, branching, whether A(x) is fixed by the singular values) points to the Sturm–Liouville / integral-equation eigenvalue setting. In that setting the question was settled. Solutions with fixed initial data are entire in λ (Poincaré). The boundary-value solution or resolvent is meromorphic: a ratio of entire functions with poles only at the eigenvalues, so there is no branching and no essential singularity (Fredholm, Hilbert's integral-equation papers, later the analytic Fredholm theorem). It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. The basic question is classical and closed, so I marked it inactive. Meromorphic continuation of resolvents is still studied in more general settings (non-compact or non-self-adjoint problems, scattering resonances), and the inverse-spectral side remains an active field, but neither is this specific question. Confidence is medium because the exact equation Hilbert had in mind is not on the page, and the search results only support the general statements, not the Fredholm/Hilbert history.
